The spin correlation function for two distinct times in a Heisenberg ferromagnet with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions under an inhomogeneous external field has been calculated. This calculation was performed within the framework of the Green function method and the stochastic cluster approximation for a cubic lattice. The derived formula for the spin correlation function expresses it as a sum of products involving the spectral functions of the corresponding transfer matrix. The transfer matrix spectral function was determined by solving a system of linear equations using the method of the finite element method. The effect of the strength of the Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions on the correlation function was examined. The obtained results were also verified using the Monte Carlo method. The spin correlation function was also analyzed in terms of temperature dependence.

The multi-robot Cooperative Trajectory Planning issue is addressed by introducing a Virtual Distributed Trajectory Planning (VDTP) system that ensures collision avoidance through a novel, linear safe corridor. The VDTP system models multi-robot motion planning as a nonlinear optimization problem, solving it by first defining constraints to maintain system stability and feasibility, and then introducing a virtual control input to define a safe corridor for each robot, ensuring that robots adhere to their corridor without violating system constraints. A modified Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm is used to solve the nonlinear optimization problem, and simulations conducted on a quadrotor swarm demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in terms of computational efficiency, feasibility, and collision avoidance.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation, specifically for tasks like semantic segmentation, faces significant challenges when adapting models from a labeled simulation environment to an unlabeled real-world setting with diverse background factors like weather and lighting conditions. This research paper presents CARLANE, a benchmark designed to assess UDA capabilities in recognizing lane markings under various real-world environmental conditions. The dataset comprises simulated images and corresponding segmentation masks along with real-world images captured in different weather and lighting conditions. The approach to evaluate UDA methods involves fine-tuning a model pre-trained on the simulated dataset using both simulated and real-world images. The performance of these methods will be assessed based on the results on the validation set and the final test set. The research aims to serve as a reference for UDA in deep learning and serve as a resource for advancing the field of semantic segmentation.

Our research examines the influence of particles on the dynamic contact angle formed on an elastic hydrogel surface. By integrating discrete particles into the surface, the equilibrium contact angle increases due to localized increases in surface stress. We've developed a mathematical model to estimate the average size and spatial arrangement of particles near the contact area, and how they impact the dynamic contact angle. The outcomes of our model align with data from experiments involving hydrogels infused with silica nanoparticles. The findings suggest that incorporating nanoparticles into hydrogels can be used to fine-tune the dynamic contact angle.

In a preceding study, we examined the association between a university's structure and its success, and found a positive correlation between students' network characteristics and academic results in the context of an online course. Building on this research, the current study aims to explore how the COVID-19 pandemic impacted this correlation, and assess whether it altered the relative importance of different network features in predicting academic achievement. Unlike our initial findings, the current study reveals a diminished correlation between academic results and network metrics, and a heightened emphasis on community-related measures in the post-pandemic data.

A new, rapid wind profiling technique has been developed utilizing L-band Doppler radar data at the 1-4 km altitude range. This technique leverages the autoregressive theory to assess the temporal variations in Doppler spread and wind velocity. By employing Doppler spectra at multiple altitudes, the technique estimates wind profiles with minimal computational demands, processed within a second. This method's reliability was tested through comparisons with radio acoustic sounding system (RASS) measurements, yielding an average relative error of 0.4 m/s. This technique's effectiveness was further demonstrated during a severe storm on July 19, 2013. This paper presents the technique's application and the corresponding wind profile measurements.

The open cluster UBC 274, which has an age of 200 million years according to a prior study, poses a significant challenge to the standard theory of how stars and gas move within the galaxy. The cluster's core is comprised of gas that has been compressed, causing the stars to spin up and the gas to form new stars at a faster rate than expected. In contrast to the expected behavior, the gas in the cluster is actually rotating in the opposite direction of the stars and gas in the surrounding region. By analyzing the movement of the gas in UBC 274, we found that the gas is not rotating in the same way as the stars. The gas in the cluster is actually being affected by the motion of the stars, causing it to slow down and become more dense. The cluster's unique properties, including its rapid gas consumption, high star formation rate and unusual gas movement, suggest that it is an example of a "suppressed' gas accretion disk. The suppressed nature of this disk is likely due to the motion of the stars, causing it to be less effective than the motion of the stars in the surrounding region.

The primary metric for assessing the quality of parallel corpora is the BLEU score, yet the human-generated parallel corpora are limited in quantity, whereas those created artificially through model-based approaches often offer a much larger dataset. This study investigates whether the large artificial corpora can be leveraged to improve metrics beyond the BLEU score, particularly in the context of multilingual settings. Contrary to the findings of previous research, our experiments reveal that artificially generated corpora can contribute positively to the assessment of corpora quality, including those with non-native languages. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that a quality score can be effectively derived from the NMT model itself by computing the BLEU score of artificial translations produced from the corpus in question.

We explore the ground state transitions in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain under the influence of engineered dissipation, where a specific pair of sites is connected to two independent reservoirs, one with antiferromagnetic coupling and the other with ferromagnetic coupling. Through numerical simulations and finite-size analysis, we examine the entanglement entropy of the bulk spins between the driven pair and the rest of the chain. We observe that the entanglement entropy exhibits distinct behaviors across different regimes of the antiferromagnetic coupling strength, including a logarithmic growth, a saturation, and a revival. We derive a comprehensive understanding of the observed phenomena within the Mott phase, and attribute the revival to the emergence of a critical phase. We also investigate the time-dependent dynamics of the entanglement, where we analyze the time-evolution of the von Neumann entropy following the drive turn-on. We observe that the entanglement revival is preceded by a transient regime, and demonstrate that the time-evolved entanglement entropy can be accurately described by a time-local Schrödinger equation.

The interaction between spin and orbit in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers is analyzed, particularly focusing on the resulting bands in the absence of inversion symmetry. Through the application of group theory, the components of the spin-orbit vector are identified, which enable the determination of spin-orbit coupling parameters for bands of any symmetry under specific conditions. This approach is demonstrated using the calculated bands from density functional theory, resulting in the derivation of spin-orbit parameters for the flat bands within the Kohn anomaly window. It is observed that these parameters exhibit non-trivial patterns in the Brillouin zone.

A new brain-inspired computing method, known as Quantum Reservoir Computing, uses quantum behavior to efficiently process information, typically through simple systems and complex interactions. To achieve this goal, researchers are exploring novel quantum architectures, such as those utilizing individual qubits. To make these small systems more useful, their limited functionality must be overcome, and their potential investigated. This study delves into the capabilities of limited qubit-based systems, and how their behavior mimics more complex systems, and how their basic properties can be used for advanced applications, such as advanced pattern recognition and data filtering.

Our research has identified the production of a high-quality, epitaxial GaN thin film on a large sapphire substrate using a specific fabrication process. By optimizing the growth conditions, we achieved high-quality, smooth surface morphology, as evidenced by atomic force microscopy. The film's optical quality was assessed through photoluminescence experiments, revealing strong, evenly distributed emission patterns. The results indicate that this method is suitable for large-scale fabrication of semiconductor nanostructures on these substrates.

This research introduces a numerical study on the use of Lagrange and mixed finite elements for solving an elliptic PDE, aiming to determine the optimal approach for a specific problem. The study employs the MFEM library, a C++ code designed for finite element mesh management and discretization. By exploring the library's capabilities, the research aims to establish a framework for comparing the efficiency of Lagrange and mixed finite elements. Furthermore, the investigation seeks to provide insights into the relative advantages and disadvantages of Lagrange and mixed finite elements, as well as the impact of mesh quality on the solution process.

We investigate the cosmological evolution of two models featuring dark energy with variable signs that interact with dark matter, with one model involving a transition in sign and the other lacking one. We find that one model exhibits a phantom-like state within a specific evolutionary phase and ultimately leads to a future Big Rip in all scenarios. Conversely, the model without the transition exhibits a future de Sitter phase and a specific type of cosmological evolution in two dimensions, characterized by the presence of scalar field oscillations. We also analyze the dynamic behavior of these models and compare their performance using a cosmological dataset, with one scenario showing better alignment and the other matching the data almost as well as the standard Lambda-CDM model.

A shock wave generated in the outflow of a supermassive black hole following a tidal disruption event pushes out the accretion column and drives it forward.  We have developed a basic model to describe the motion of the column at a time when the shock wave is strong and moves perpendicular to the column's direction.  The acceleration provided by the shock wave causes the column to rapidly move forward, a phenomenon that can be observed as a burst of radio waves.  The speed of the radio wave burst is determined by the speed at which the column is accelerating along the shock wave, a speed which is roughly equivalent to the speed of light.  The duration of the radio wave burst is determined by the time it takes for the shock wave to propagate through the column and cause it to expand.  The model predicts a burst of radio waves that is observable for a relatively short time, a time that is dependent on the speed of the motion of the column and the thickness of the column.  The model suggests that a burst of radio waves, a burst lasting a matter of minutes, could be observable for a period of time that is comparable to the speed of light.

This research introduces a new computational technique for analyzing the interaction between acoustic waves and small micro-spheres within a fluid, taking into account the complex interactions between the sphere and the surrounding fluid. A mathematical model is developed to describe the time-varying behavior of the sphere and the fluid, which is then solved using a numerical method that produces highly accurate results. The method is applied to a specific case study of a 10 micron radius polystyrene micro-sphere submerged in water, subjected to an external acoustic wave, and the results are compared against experimental findings. The technique is also adaptable for simulating the behavior of micro-bubbles and micro-emulsions in such acoustic interactions.

In recent years, the field of emotional cognitive assessment has garnered significant interest. The assessment of emotional intelligence, a key area of research, involves analyzing a person's ability to recognize, interact, and manage emotions in themselves and others. This study focuses on developing emotional cognition as a self-contained skill, drawing from the principles of cognitive psychology. The proposed approach incorporates a multi-modal model, leveraging face, speech, and text as input modalities. The model's audio component is represented using a deep speech encoder, while the facial expressions are encoded using a combination of a pre-trained model and a text-based model. The text modality is represented using a transformer. The model's parameter space is shared across its various components, allowing for efficient learning. The model's effectiveness is evaluated using the IEMOCAP dataset, with the goal of identifying emotional states. The dataset comprises three sub-datasets, each requiring a specific task to be solved. The results obtained from the model are compared with those of the current state-of-the-art models, demonstrating the model's superior performance. The model's auxiliary task, emotion acknowledgment, is also evaluated and found to enhance the model's performance in multi-task learning.

The rapid growth of autonomous vehicles technology has led to a significant increase in simulations-based validation methods. To create realistic simulations, developers rely on digital twins that combine detailed 3D models and simulated environmental behaviors. However, defining environmental behaviors requires defining rules that govern interactions between vehicles and their surroundings, a task that's particularly challenging when considering the bird's-eye view as a 2D grid may not accurately capture complex terrain features. To facilitate the definition of these rules, we've developed PanGEA, a free and open-source annotation tool that empowers users to define and visualize 2D bird's-eye view rules, 3D geometry, and terrain features. Leveraging the OpenDR framework, PanGEA also enables users to seamlessly export and integrate these definitions into autonomous systems.

We have developed a modified version of the downsizing model, which takes into account the varying initial mass functions for elliptical galaxies and the occurrence of type Ia supernovae. The results indicate that the star formation periods for elliptical galaxies are significantly shorter than previously calculated, specifically between 0.3 and 0.5 billion years. The inclusion of type Ia supernovae in the model's chemical evolution calculations is essential for achieving the observed mass-metallicity relationship for elliptical galaxies. The variation in initial mass functions among galaxies is primarily driven by the diversity in star formation durations, ages, and metallicities, rather than their mass. This variation is also the primary cause of the observed bimodality in the [O/Fe]-[Mg/Fe] plane. The model suggests that the cosmic evolution of elliptical galaxies can be divided into three stages: a brief star formation period, a period of chemical evolution, and a period of chemical homogenization due to type Ia supernovae. The model's predictions are in line with observed data, indicating that the star formation periods for elliptical galaxies are significantly shorter than those for spiral galaxies.

A novel approach to image compressive sensing (CS) is proposed, which combines the strengths of $\ell_0$ sparsity and cluster-based feature extraction. The method involves two main steps: first, sparse representations of images are calculated using a cluster-based model, and second, sparse codes are obtained by solving a non-linear optimization problem that incorporates cluster-wise $\ell_0$ sparsity and total variation (TV) regularization. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the use of synthetic and real-world images, with the results showing superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art CS methods.

The human face is comprised of numerous distinct regions, each bearing signs of specific diseases, making accurate identification of these areas crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment. This study presents a novel method for segmenting the face and annotating individual segments based on specific health issues. Our approach involves training a segmentation model to group facial features into distinct areas, then processing each region separately to identify specific health issues. This region-specific model utilizes a multi-modal framework, combining spatial features, disease-related features, and historical information to accurately diagnose various conditions. Our model outperforms previous methods in identifying five distinct facial health issues.

Our research delves into the efficiency of sequential decoding for polarized accumulation codes (PAC codes), a class that includes DA codes. Although DA codes have been extensively studied, PAC codes were only recently introduced due to computational limitations in analyzing their structural properties. We have developed efficient decoding methods for PAC codes, yielding precise assessments of the maximum likelihood decoding error probability and the average error rate of belief propagation decoding, as well as a more efficient search space for maximum likelihood decoding. Our findings indicate that the complexity of best-path belief propagation decoding is significantly reduced, making it a viable and efficient alternative to maximum likelihood decoding.

Online recommender systems have become increasingly vital in modern digital services, delivering personalized content to millions of users daily.  However, they are often hindered by the "cold-start" problem, which arises when users or items are unknown, making it difficult to generate effective recommendations. To mitigate this, systems often rely on suggestions, aiming to help users discover new items. This study focuses on addressing the challenge posed by cold-start users, particularly by analyzing how their interests evolve over time and developing a new approach to handle this transition. The proposed system, called Meta-Transitional Learning, incorporates a memory structure to capture user preferences, a pre-training method to refine item representations, and a two-stage learning process to optimize user and item transitions. By adapting to users' evolving preferences, the system provides more accurate and relevant item suggestions, ultimately enhancing user engagement. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset reveal that the proposed system outperforms existing benchmarks, delivering notable improvements in click-through rates and recall, with a significant increase of 3.59% in CTR and 1.91% in recall.

This article provides a comprehensive review of the historical development and current understanding of ultra high energy astrophysical phenomena, with a focus on the acceleration and propagation of high-energy photons, as well as their observation and theoretical interpretation.

A new theoretical model, known as the Impactor Momentum Transfer Model (IMTM), has been developed to analyze the dynamic interaction between a space object and an incoming projectile. This model, based on a rigorous mathematical framework, accurately predicts the momentum transferred to the target object, allowing for a detailed understanding of the resulting deformation and velocity. A key aspect of the model is the inclusion of the target's reaction to the impact, which significantly affects the momentum transfer and target response. This novel model, with its focus on the projectile's shape, offers a significant improvement over existing impact theories and methods, especially in the context of space missions involving impacters. This includes the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), which relies on a precise calculation of the momentum transferred to evaluate the effectiveness of the impact.

Driver identification through facial and vehicular features is a critical aspect of
autonomous vehicles. In this research, a novel image fusion technique is developed
to enhance the performance of the MuSykleNet model, specifically designed for
through-the-windshield driver recognition. The unification of multiple images from
different frequency domains improves the accuracy of driver identification,
yielding an average accuracy of 99.6%. The resulting model, dubbed MU-Net, is a
highly efficient solution for real-time through-the-windshield driver
identification.

This study examines the website content for prominent open-source programming languages, uncovering a lesser-known aspect - extensive description sections. Our research, the first to study this element, has analyzed the 100 most popular repositories on GitHub, including Python, JavaScript, and C. Our analysis of these text fields reveals a pattern of users seeking information on package suitability, purposes, and benefits through search terms. Our findings suggest that concise, relevant descriptions enhance discoverability. Furthermore, we've identified inconsistencies in description usage, highlighting potential improvements for developers and maintainers. Our results provide a foundation for future research and inform best practices for website design.

Covariate selection is a widespread challenge in regression analysis, and the issue of missing data is also a common occurrence. To address these problems, we propose a novel estimator that integrates multistage penalization techniques with multiple imputation methods to recover lost information from both missing covariates and outcomes. Our approach yields a reliable estimator at a manageable computational cost, and its asymptotic performance is supported by theoretical guarantees. Derived from this concept is a penalized two-stage least squares estimator that minimizes the risk of the $L_1$-norm by leveraging the imputation of missing covariates. Also considered are multistage $L_1$- and $L_0$-estimators for cases where the number of covariates exceeds the sample size, and the associated numerical results confirm the method's effectiveness.

The accuracy of approximations using the inverse hyperbolic tangent function for the first kind complete elliptic integral has been extensively studied. Two specific hypotheses have been put forth by researchers, including Gauss and Legendre. This research aims to prove that the second hypothesis, proposed by Legendre, is indeed valid. Additionally, we present a novel expansion of the complete elliptic integral, which incorporates the inverse hyperbolic tangent function. This expansion provides a more precise approximation than existing methods.

Deep learning models are typically trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised techniques.  While supervised methods like supervised learning are effective, they are limited by the need for labelled data.  To address this challenge, researchers have developed unsupervised algorithms that can help to improve the accuracy of supervised models by identifying underlying patterns in data.  However, these methods often struggle to adapt to new datasets and require significant time and computational power.  To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel approach, called Decomposed Inductive Method (DIM), which leverages the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised techniques to create more accurate and efficient learning methods.  By decomposing the complex problem of data representation into more manageable sub-problems and solving each one independently, DIM enables the discovery of more accurate and relevant features, leading to enhanced performance on a wide range of tasks.  Our approach is particularly well-suited to large-scale datasets and can be easily integrated with existing supervised and unsupervised methods.  We have successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of DIM through its ability to improve the accuracy of supervised models on various image classification tasks while requiring less labelled data.

The rapid expansion of social media platforms has enabled users to easily share and disseminate diverse news items. This has given rise to concerns over the credibility of news sources, with fake news posing a significant threat to public trust. To address this issue, we investigate methods for automatically detecting English and Arabic fake news using supervised learning approaches. Our study compares the effectiveness of various cutting-edge deep learning architectures, including traditional convolutional neural networks, to a cutting-edge transformer-based approach. The proposed experiments examine the utility of multiple classification using distinct fake news types as classes and demonstrate that our top-performing model achieves a high overall accuracy of 98.7% on the associated dataset.

The original paper where this article is a continuation originally investigated torsion groups of rational elliptic curves within specific quadratic Galois fields over the rational numbers. These specific fields are generated by fourth-degree cyclotomic polynomials, denoted as $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{4^n})$. The current paper expands on this by examining the torsion groups of rational elliptic curves over a broader, larger field, represented as $\mathbb{Q}(\Sigma_{4^n})$, which is formed by the combination of all the mentioned quadratic fields. The text then proceeds to correct a previously stated assertion regarding the field $\mathbb{Q}(\Sigma_{4^n})$, specifically that it is equivalent to the field generated by the rational numbers and the fourth cyclotomic polynomial, denoted as $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{4^n})$.

The interconnected properties of complex qubits are a topic of investigation for their potential role in mimicking neural processing. However, the delicate nature of these connections is disrupted by random noise, which has a profound impact on their behavior. To gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, we have developed a simulation method that utilizes matrix product operators to model complex qubit interactions. Our research reveals that even minimal amounts of noise can have a profound impact on these systems, causing them to exhibit more pronounced correlations than expected, particularly in systems with multiple qubits. Notably, the influence of noise in these systems is not solely localized, but rather has far-reaching effects that can be observed in regions distant from the point of introduction.

The objective of our research is to automate the decision-making process for which URLs to crawl next during the web scraping phase, by utilizing an RL agent that focuses on specific branches within the URLs' HTML document structure. To enhance the training efficiency of this agent, we introduce a variant of the Q-learning algorithm, called the Adaptive Target Policy (ATP) Model, which allows agents to quickly grasp the web scraping strategy. We have thoroughly evaluated the performance of this branch-based RL approach in comparison to conventional RL methods, as well as in contrast to the current state-of-the-art RL algorithms for web scraping, demonstrating its superiority on two distinct datasets.

We suggest a straightforward yet efficient method for establishing relationships between specific events, defined by properties and outcomes. This approach enables the creation of a unified structure for various types of events, covering both significant and minor occurrences. By standardizing event relationships, we can derive and categorize different scenarios and adaptations based on an initial event setting. The proposed system is flexible enough to accommodate a wide range of event types, as demonstrated by implementations utilizing both imperative and declarative programming languages.

A novel, fast, and memory-efficient method for restoring wavefields has been developed. This approach utilizes limited-subspace weighted matrix decompositions to break down large, ill-conditioned or singular matrices. Unlike traditional methods, it can provide a solution with minimal back-projection costs, even in the case of singular matrices. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated by applying it to the reverse time migration and Born-Von Karman integral equations. As a comparison, it shows significant improvements in computational efficiency and reduced memory usage.

Metalenses have been widely researched for their ability to condense light into a small focal spot on a sensor, eliminating the need for traditional lens-based optics. However, they are limited by their narrow frequency range and narrow field of view. In this research, we have developed metalenses with a large field of view of 30 degrees and frequency ranges of 400-500nm and 500-700nm. Using computational design, we have optimized the structure of these metalenses to achieve high resolution across a wide range of wavelengths and to focus light into a small focal spot. The results show that these metalenses have high resolution and a wide field of view, making them suitable for use in endoscopes. The findings of this research can be applied to the design of metalenses with a large field of view and wide frequency range.

The study of radio-frequency atmospheric pressure discharges has been conducted using a coupled computational approach that includes multi-physics simulations and a self-consistent model. The coupled multiphysics simulations have been carried out to investigate the behavior of radio-frequency discharges at varying input powers and frequencies, and reveal a complex interplay between electrical characteristics, gas temperature, and plasma chemistry. These simulations have been compared to a self-consistent model that predicts discharge regime transitions, and show good agreement with experimental findings at low power levels. However, the high-power data shows a shift towards the filamentary regime, and this is attributed to gas breakdown and the resulting increase in gas temperature. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for gas breakdown and the non-equilibrium nature of gas temperature in modeling the behavior of radio-frequency atmospheric pressure discharges.

This research examines the impact of string theory corrections on the eikonal frequency and shadow of $d$-dimensional black holes with toroidal compactification. The frequency and shadow's dependence on the compactification dimensions' number $n$ is investigated, along with the influence of the string theory correction parameter $\alpha$ and the angular number $l$. The results show that as $\alpha$ increases, the frequency decreases, and for large $n$, the frequency remains unaffected. Additionally, the radius of the shadow expands with an increase in $\alpha$ and $n$.

The gravitational waves produced by compact binary mergers can be detected indirectly by analyzing data from pulsar timing arrays, thanks to the precise pulse signals sent out by pulsars. Two effective methods for identifying these signals are the common-spectrum and cross-correlation searches. To compare the effectiveness of these methods, researchers have conducted a simulation based on real data from the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, evaluating how well both methods can identify a hypothetical gravitational wave signal. The results show that the signal's detectability using the common-spectrum method is about 30% better than with the cross-correlation approach. This improved performance is due to the ability of the common-spectrum method to analyze a wider range of potential signal locations within the pulsar network. The results also suggest that common-spectrum searches can be run more efficiently by analyzing data from the pulsar network in smaller groups, or'subarrays'.

The condition for a matrix to be a suitable generator matrix for orthonormal codes with a particular length and dimension can be determined using two distinct criteria. The reason for the presence of duplicate criteria lies in the complex relationship between the structure of generator matrices and the presence of non-trivial cycles in their corresponding parity-check matrices. Additionally, sufficient conditions have been established for the corresponding generator matrices of full-dimensional partial spread codes to exist, with specific requirements imposed on the row weights and column sums of the parity-check matrices.

This research paper presents the concept of a truncated Toeplitz operator with multiple channels, constructed using functions that are not necessarily bounded. The construction of these operators, built on functions from the Hardy space in n-dimensional complex space, involves the use of kernels and is shown to be equivalent to existing TTOs when extended using a specific approach. The equivalence is established through an isometric relation between the norms of these operators, which is achieved by finding a suitable metric on a specific space of functions.

Sequential experiments, a widely used research design in numerous fields, is rapidly gaining traction due to the advancements in online learning and bandit-based methods. These methods are often built upon the empirical Bayes approach, a design principle that enables the creation of an optimal decision rule through the estimation of a Bayesian posterior. This study delves into the practical implications of sequential experiments, focusing on the concept of influence functions to assess the impact of outliers on the Bayesian estimator. By employing influence functions, we can identify and detect outliers within the Bayesian framework. Moreover, we propose a novel approach to robust estimation, one that is theoretically grounded and can be executed efficiently. Our framework is demonstrated to be effective in a real-world setting, as we develop an influence function-based algorithm to detect and flag anomalous data in a real-world clinical trial.

Incorporating an unsupervised anomaly detection model into autonomous vehicles poses significant challenges, particularly when training and operational data have different underlying characteristics. This paper presents an unsupervised approach to clustering sensor data, utilizing dimensionality reduction and visual analysis with UMAP to facilitate inspection and evaluation. By applying this method to audio data from two distinct sensors on a single vehicle, we demonstrate the efficacy of UMAP in identifying sensor anomalies and distinguishing between sensor types with distinct physical properties.

A novel ferromagnetic state is discovered in a spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Fermi gas with a sparse SU(N) pseudospin degree of freedom, where N is greater than two. This ferromagnetic state arises from a spin-polarized region separated by a high-temperature, paramagnetic phase. The presence of the sparse level crosses links these regions, enabling the system to transition between different areas via hopping. Calculations of the system's spectral properties and mobility reveal that its behavior is analogous to that of a tight-binding lattice.

The primary goal of our study is to investigate the potential of using stacking methods to identify pulsars detectable by the Fermi Large Area Telescope that may be hidden from radio telescopes due to absorption. To accomplish this, we created a sample of 1,430 gamma-ray pulsars located near the Galactic plane. Next, we applied three distinct stacking methods to these pulsars, using coordinates, radio beam coverage, and electron density along lines of sight. Calculations of false discovery rates revealed that approximately one thousand pulsars could be detected by each method without discovering any actual pulsars. Notably, the most effective method, based on radio beam coverage, suggests the possibility of discovering pulsars detectable by Fermi, such as PSR J1023+56, that experiences less beam overlap. Furthermore, our study found that approximately one hundred thousand pulsars could potentially be detected by the Fermi telescope across the entire Galactic plane. The results of our study demonstrate the stacking technique's utility in discovering previously unknown gamma-ray pulsars.

In the study of two-dimensional electrons confined by an effective potential, we investigate the influence of an external magnetic field on their low-energy excitations. It is well-established that when this confinement is weak, the system's low-energy manifolds can be accurately described by the Schrödinger--Poisson model. Our research reveals that when the confinement is stronger, the system's low-energy manifolds can be approximated using the fractional quantum Hall Hamiltonian with modified edge properties. Importantly, we derive the general form of the edge properties and the system's low-energy excitations in the presence of both a strong and a weak potential barrier. Our findings demonstrate that the low-energy excitations exhibit a more intricate structure than initially thought, with the potential to impact the transport properties of the system.

The Intense Energy Events (IEE) experiment, conducted at the Beam Test Facility in Frascati, Italy, focuses on measuring the electromagnetic radiation emitted by beams of protons or heavy ions during intense energy events, specifically Total Energy Loss (TEL) or Bremsstrahlung processes. A key objective of this experiment is to measure radiation levels in extreme conditions, potentially applicable to high-energy atmospheric events, supernovae, and gamma-ray bursts, as well as to test radiation shielding concepts in future space missions. The instrument package, designed to fit a single flight unit, consists of three main components: a silicon detector for measuring X-ray radiation, a plastic scintillator for detecting photons and electrons across various energy ranges, and an electron multiplier for measuring high-energy electron rates. A data acquisition system with real-time data analysis is utilized to process the collected data. The experiment has been successfully tested with proton beams of up to 300 MeV and electron beams of up to 1 GeV, yielding satisfactory results. This paper outlines the experiment's performance, obtained from data collected using 300 MeV protons and 1 GeV electrons.

This paper explores the truncated Cauchy problem for the Boltzmann equation, specifically when the initial density and velocity are both zero. The existence of a unique global solution is demonstrated for this problem under the assumption of weak collisions, provided that the collision strength meets a certain threshold. The findings indicate that even with minimal initial data, solutions can experience significant growth in the $L^1$ norm within a short time frame of $0$ to $t$. Furthermore, it is shown that the collision strength must be less than or equal to $1/3$ for the linear growth of the $L^1$ norm to be possible. The study also reveals the exponential growth of the $H^1$ norm of the solution, provided the collision strength meets a certain threshold. The findings of this study generalize previous results obtained by Desvillettes and Lemarie-Mihajevskaya, specifically those related to the Cauchy problem for the Boltzmann equation with a small initial density.

The presence of label noise in real-world datasets poses significant challenges to deep neural networks, compromising their ability to generalize effectively. To mitigate this issue, our proposed approach involves the integration of robust classifiers with robust training methods. By combining these strategies, we aim to achieve resilience to label noise in real-world data. We have developed a new method, known as "Soft-Bias", designed to minimize the impact of noisy labels on training data. This approach leverages the use of probabilistic loss functions, such as Kullback-Leibler divergence and Cross Entropy, to optimize model performance. Furthermore, we have employed techniques such as label smoothing and dual-loss to enhance the robustness of our models during the training process. Our findings indicate that combining these strategies results in a noticeable improvement in the accuracy of classifiers in noisy label settings.

A construction called orbit codes was introduced by Katz and Katz in 2013, which combines an action of a finite group and a code construction method. In this research, the automorphism ensembles of orbit codes are examined, including a specific set of codes known as cyclic orbit codes. An approximation of the dimension of the automorphism group's image for cyclic orbit codes is established, which helps identify when the automorphism group can be isometric to the full automorphism group of the code. Additionally, the conditions under which the automorphism group can be isometric to the full automorphism group of the code for cyclic orbit codes are determined.

A star in the oldest open cluster M67 has been identified, with its mass analyzed for the first time. The star exhibits characteristics of a main-sequence star but is expected to be an older subgiant. The star's age was determined using isochrone analysis of the cluster's main sequence and turnoff region, placing it at $0.95 \pm 0.10\,{\rm Gyr}$. The star's luminosity, effective temperature, and composition were also measured, confirming it as a high-precision standard reference for astrophysical calibration. The star's mass was then calculated using stellar evolution models, yielding a value of $1.21 \pm 0.10\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. The mass obtained from the model matches predictions from asteroseismology and spectroscopy, validating the use of this star as a standard reference. The analysis highlights the benefits of observing with the K2 mission and incorporating high-precision spectroscopy, particularly for studying the evolution of the lower-mass stars in the future.

A novel, modified version of the SPH method, specifically designed for hydrodynamics simulations, has been formulated. This version, named MP-SPH, aims to resolve issues associated with the original SPH, such as volume and gradient calculations, by introducing a multi-particle approach. This approach utilizes the concept of finite difference to calculate volume and gradient, and a multi-particle average to determine the entropy and entropy flux. This results in improved volume and gradient accuracy, and the entropy equation remains consistent. This work presents the new formulation, demonstrates its advantages through numerical examples, and highlights its potential to serve as a starting point for a more advanced method.

Capturing high-quality spectra is crucial in various fields, including chemistry and biology, but current methods are limited by high costs, time-consuming processes, and the need for precise measurements. To overcome these challenges, researchers have developed a novel algorithm for reconstructing spectra based on low-cost, low-resolution images captured under different illumination conditions. This algorithm, known as the Pixel-sensitive Deep Function-blend Network (PDFN), leverages deep learning to estimate high-quality spectra from any number of images. By analyzing the images using a custom feature map, PDFN can estimate the intensity of individual pixels and reconstruct the spectrum, even in areas with poor signal quality, using a series of interconnected neural networks. Extensive testing on real-world and simulated datasets demonstrates that PDFN outperforms current methods and remains highly accurate when dealing with high levels of noise and data distortion.

In computer vision, a significant issue is determining the location tags of objects within large-scale databases. To address this, our research introduces Context Sensitive Object Geotagging (CSOG), an innovative method that leverages extensive datasets to pinpoint object locations within complex outdoor scenes. The CSOG approach relies on the concept of context, which is learned from the co-occurring objects within an image, to infer the location of the target object. This is achieved through a process where the interrelationships between objects within a context window are analyzed using a graph-based framework. The method then utilizes spatial constraints to predict the location of the target object. The CSOG approach has been successfully implemented on the Cambridge in the Wild (CIW) dataset, yielding impressive results, with an accuracy rate of 77.2% in localizing objects, even when the target object is partially hidden or in complex outdoor environments.

The retrieval of water volume in dam reservoirs from satellite images has become an essential task, particularly in the context of monitoring Earth's natural resources. This study introduces a novel, straightforward, and universally applicable approach to calculate the stored water volume in dams from satellite images using both spectral and spatial data. Initially, the study area is segmented into patches, and a customized metric learning technique is employed to enhance the quality of water mask classification. This involves combining the results of two classification models, one trained on spectral data and the other on textural data, to improve classification accuracy. Next, the study area is divided into square tiles, and a neural network is trained to predict water body class labels within each pixel using the patch labels. The network is trained on a customized metric, and its performance is evaluated using a loss function that combines classification and regression aspects. This approach is validated on two datasets, one built from satellite images of the Costa Rica reservoir and the other from the public UC Merced landuse dataset. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over traditional classification-based methods, and the integration of regression-based methods, and show its robustness to noise.

This paper presents a fiscally constrained subfield of the Frobenius extension of a polynomial ring over a field, known as the QFS-module. We explore its inherent features, prove the modules' stability under extension and, making an assumption, establish that any non-trivial QFS-module possesses a maximal fiscally constrained submodule. A special case, where the field is finite, reveals that any non-empty collection of non-zero polynomials, partially summing to zero, forms a QFS-module. Consequently, we establish that their sum generates a QFS-module as well.

In online commerce, product category prediction plays a significant role in both text and image forms. Our research focuses on predicting the point of attraction, a key aspect of product categories that indicates whether an item is a detail or summary of another product. We introduce a multi-modal approach combining text and image features to improve performance in this task, utilizing transformer and multi-modal architectures. Our experimental results on a dataset of 1,500 categories show that our multi-modal model outperforms its single-modal counterparts, with notable improvements in both macro and micro averaging precision.

This research delves into the relationship between investor inquiries raised during corporate conference calls and subsequent stock price changes. By examining 25,557 questions for a 1-year period across 1,502 publicly listed companies, our analysis uncovers significant insights regarding the impact of these inquiries on stock prices. Our findings demonstrate that a substantial portion of investor questions are connected to future operational or earnings outcomes, and their relevance can significantly influence the stock price movement. Furthermore, our study shows that shares experience notable, significant price fluctuations in response to relevant questions. By examining the predictive value of these inquiries, our analysis reveals that shares tend to rise after investors ask questions with positive tone and ask few questions on operational-related topics. Our investigation also finds that shares tend to decline after investors pose questions with negative tone and ask many questions on operational-related topics. By employing a novel text-based stock price prediction model that incorporates the predictive power of both the tone and the topic of investor inquiries, our study demonstrates that shares exhibit improved predictive ability when both factors are considered. Our analysis further indicates that shares experience considerable, significant price fluctuations in response to conference calls. By modeling the predictive performance of such inquiries, our study demonstrates that shares benefit from increased predictive ability when conference calls are factored into the prediction model.

Optimal sensor placement is a critical issue in designing efficient wireless sensor networks, requiring careful balance between coverage, deployment, and resource utilization. Existing research has primarily focused on uniform communication ranges, but real-world sensor networks often exhibit varying signal strengths, rendering uniform placement ineffective. This paper explores sensor placement in heterogeneous wireless networks, where signal strength varies across sensors, leading to non-uniform communication ranges. Building on its predecessor, which addressed homogeneous networks, the approach utilizes Monte-Carlo simulations to estimate coverage sets and determines the minimum number of sensors needed for full network coverage. Additionally, an analytical model has been developed to optimize sensor density, minimizing deployment costs while achieving desired coverage levels, ensuring that nearby sensors don't overlap, and preventing over-provisioning. Extensive simulations have validated the approach's efficacy in optimizing sensor networks, offering significant cost savings without compromising coverage.

Researchers have developed a complex quantum filter, leveraging the eigenvalues of an analytic function to achieve a desired filter outcome. This technique requires precise control and is computationally intensive, requiring multiple matrix multiplications. To overcome these limitations, a new approach is presented, which relies on polynomial coefficients rather than complex analysis. The new filter offers equivalent performance to its predecessor, but with a crucial advantage - it necessitates fewer matrix multiplications on a quantum processor. Building on this framework, a hybrid method for solving quantum linear systems is proposed. This method combines the strengths of quantum and classical computations, and is optimized for efficiency. Numerical experiments have shown that the new approach is robust and can effectively handle high-dimensional problems.

The infant skyrmion is a fundamental topological excitation in two-dimensional systems and plays a key role in the phase transition of two-dimensional superfluids. Our research reveals that compact infant skyrmions are a topological feature unique to two-dimensional systems and cannot exist in three-dimensional space. We have discovered a novel phenomenon where self-dual compact infant skyrmions emerge in nonlinear substances with specific properties. By applying a self-dual constraint, we have successfully created and visualized self-dual compact infant skyrmions in two-dimensional systems. Our findings have significant implications for the study of topological excitations, nonlinear dynamics, and quantum physics.

This research explores novel phenomena beyond the Standard Model, within a well-established framework called the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). By analyzing a set of key interactions, we aim to understand their properties and behavior, as well as any potential limitations that may impact our findings. Our study delves into the role these interactions play in shaping the evolution of fundamental particles at high energy levels, as well as their potential effects in future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and its upgraded future incarnation. Furthermore, we examine the unique effects these interactions may have on various particle decays, including a specific process involving a Standard Model particle called the W boson.

We report on an exhibit showcasing a rotating diamond gyroscope and its response to various environmental changes, illustrating the impact of the Diamond Sled Gyro (DiSG). DiSG features a rotating diamond gyroscope with a 1.5 mm thickness that exhibits uniaxial rotation, allowing it to detect torque and directional changes. The diamond gyroscope is mounted on a motorized axis and can be operated in a vacuum environment, making it highly responsive to external forces. By exhibiting these properties to the public, DiSG offers a unique insight into the cutting-edge technologies used in quantum sensing and micro-nanotechnology.

The development of whole-cell models is a complex task driven by the need to understand the detailed mechanisms of cellular function. This effort has gained momentum over the past few years, aiming to create comprehensive models that can be simulated on computer algorithms. The 2019 special issue of PLOS Computational Biology was focused on recent advancements in this field. In this review, we will summarize the key findings from this collection of research papers, which showcased new approaches, updates, and refinements in the whole-cell simulation area, including new methods, software tools, and the integration of new data and findings.

Picture retrieval, a fundamental computer vision task with numerous practical applications, has garnered significant attention in the field. The development of portable vision systems necessitates the use of compact local features that facilitate effective picture retrieval. This study investigates the performance of various image descriptors on a comprehensive dataset compiled from the internet, focusing particularly on a subset depicting real-world objects. The proposed dataset, comprising 1.2 million images, is categorized based on 1,115 object classes, providing a rich source of multi-view information for picture retrieval purposes. The results indicate that convolutional neural network-based descriptors achieve superior performance, with the slow Fermi descriptor exhibiting exceptional speed and efficacy, especially when applied to query images with limited views.

Epileptic seizures are a recurring health issue, affecting a significant portion of people, with a notable 20-30% percent still experiencing them despite treatment. Utilizing machine learning to recognize seizure patterns in EEG data could greatly benefit patients, allowing them to manage their condition more effectively. However, the variability in seizure patterns at different stages and varying patient populations hinders the performance of conventional machine learning algorithms, which are often data and memory-intensive, requiring significant training times and large storage space. To overcome these limitations, we propose the use of a new approach, leveraging Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) to develop a more efficient seizure detection system. Our findings show that HDC-based learning can achieve better results than traditional shallow learning methods, with a notable improvement in classification accuracy, specifically 95.0% for normal control and atonic seizure patterns, and 92.1% for complex partial seizure patterns, when utilizing 200 seconds of EEG data.

The detection of merging black holes by the LIGO/Virgo Collaboration has opened up a new field in gravitational wave research, offering a potential tool for measuring cosmic distances and understanding the universe's expansion. By analyzing the redshifts of binary black hole events, researchers can infer the distribution of dark matter in the universe. A recent study examined the feasibility of using this method with future gravitational wave observations, focusing on how different detection methods affect the accuracy of cosmic distance measurements. Additionally, the study proposed a new approach to using gravitational wave observations to constrain models of the universe's expansion history and presents preliminary results. Furthermore, the study suggests a method to use gravitational wave observations as a means of constraining the Hubble parameter and other parameters in the Hubble Constant puzzle.

We introduce an expanded version of QALD-9, a collection of 509 questions in English, related to DBpedia and Wikidata knowledge bases. The questions in the original dataset were initially written by students as part of a 2014 CLEF evaluation campaign. The new collection, named QALD-9-plus, adds 509 additional questions in nine languages, carefully selected and translated by native speakers to query the same resources. The purpose of this expanded resource is to enable the evaluation of cross-lingual knowledge retrieval systems that can respond to questions in multiple languages. The contribution also includes a detailed analysis of the translation process and a report on a pilot query translation task using the new collection.

Human perception is inherently fragmented, with multiple viewpoints converging towards a common understanding. This process of reconciling disparate perspectives is crucial for fostering mutual understanding and cooperation. Our research introduces the Executive Ability, a simple model that optimizes the integration of partial information to synthesize a comprehensive scene representation. This is achieved by leveraging a contrastive value function, which measures the discrepancy between the current view and the anticipated outcome, with the goal of minimizing the expected difference between consecutive perceptions. The proposed approach also incorporates a resampling and relabelling mechanism, guided by a resampling function that evaluates the value of acquiring new information and a relabeling function that adjusts the labeling of existing information. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in synthesizing 3D scenes from sequential 2D views, with impressive results in both spatial and semantic accuracy.

Detecting and mitigating innate biases in AI-driven medical image analysis
is a pressing concern. Given the limitations of current data sets, which often
contain inherent biases, the need for fairness in medical imaging is increasingly
important. Innate biases, which are present in the data itself, can only be
addressed by developing and utilising data sets free from these biases. To this
end, our research introduces a novel method for identifying innate biases in medical
image collections. By employing a generative model to simulate synthetic images
and measuring the differences between real and simulated images, our approach
enables the detection of biases in image collections. Through the application of
our method to a collection of chest X-rays, its effectiveness in detecting innate
biases is demonstrated.

This study tackles the issue of noisy metric learning in information retrieval, which is a common real-world scenario where queries and documents have distinct embeddings but incorrect labels lead to noisy data. We introduce a novel loss function, called Gentle Proxy-Anchors loss, which is a more efficient alternative to proxy-anchor loss and can handle the challenges of noisy data more effectively. The proposed loss function, which is based on a two-layer neural network, can be optimized using straightforward optimization techniques, along with a sampling approach to address the high computational complexity. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets, Human-annotated and Noisy WebText datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in achieving better performance in noisy metric learning tasks.

The two-point correlation function of a function $f$ and the logarithmic derivative of the matter density $\nabla\varrho$ has been used to understand the structure of cosmic matter. By introducing a new weighted correlation relation, we have found that this function provides a more accurate representation of cosmic structure. By applying this new relation to large-scale galaxy surveys, we have found that it provides a more accurate representation of cosmic structure on small scales. Additionally, we have used this new relation to place new constraints on the growth of cosmic matter, and found that they are competitive with traditional methods. Interestingly, we have found that this new constraint is not affected by the nature of dark energy, even though it is related to the structure of cosmic matter.

A theoretical model of a topological superfluid is proposed, characterized by an SO(5) symmetry within which the Dirac mass acquires a momentum dependence, causing a gap in the bulk but closing at the boundary, giving rise to a Majorana zero mode that pairs up to form a Majoron, a long-range order that spans the system and breaks power-law scaling. This model's framework can be applied to superconducting and insulating materials, as well as to ultracold atomic communities.

A novel type of photodetector called MAPD (Monolithic Avalanche Photodiode) boasts high sensitivity and a wide dynamic range, making it a top choice for detecting low-intensity signals. However, its performance can be compromised by a phenomenon known as "snowstorm" - a condition where a single photon triggers multiple photons, released in rapid succession. To address this issue, a new class of photodetectors, called MAPD-type snowstorm photodetectors, has been developed. This innovation enables true counting of individual photons, significantly enhancing the detector's overall performance. Key features of MAPD-type snowstorm photodetectors include their ability to delay the avalanche by a predetermined time, allowing each photon to trigger a unique event. This delay is achieved by introducing an additional component in the photodetector's structure, effectively creating a "memory" that retains information about the last registered photon.

For every fixed integer d greater than or equal to 0, we propose a standard method to build a d-dimensional localized NCDG singularity, and we use this approach to examine the properties of such localized NCDG singularities with specific dimensions. We establish that for d equal to or greater than e, a d-dimensional localized NCDG singularity satisfies the condition that its g-environment is a d-e-dimensional localized GCDG singularity, and we prove that the g-environment for d less than e is uniquely a GCDG singularity. Additionally, we show that the grade of the g-minimal Cohen-Macaulay algebra associated with a d-dimensional localized NCDG singularity equals d minus e, and provide a complete algebraic description of this particular type of GCDG singularity.

A key challenge in creating new magnetic materials is achieving a balance between the need for strong magnetic strength and sufficient thermal stability. To address this, our team has developed a novel method of enhancing magnetic properties in bismuth titanate materials. By introducing iron ions, we observed significant improvements in magnetic properties at high pressures up to 4 GPa, as evidenced by nuclear forward scattering measurements. Our research revealed that the material's magnetic behavior remains stable at high pressures and temperatures up to 50 K, making it a promising candidate for future applications.

To provide investors with valuable insights, we developed a statistical framework for analyzing the trading costs of broker algorithms. Leveraging a large dataset of multiple brokers' performance, we employ a Bayesian hierarchical model to analyze individual broker's characteristics. This comprehensive model accounts for various factors, including the time of day, execution price, and market fluctuations, while considering shared and unique event characteristics. For each broker, we estimate key features such as trading cost, average order size, and entry/exit price thresholds along with event-level trade costs. To facilitate comparison and validation, we propose a ranking metric that enables the calculation of a probability difference and visually rank brokers for investor reference.

Optomechanical devices have the potential to enhance the interaction between light and matter within optical circuits. The development of advanced add-drop filters is crucial for creating complex networks of integrated photonics, and this work presents a new concept - an optomechanical device capable of forming a fully configurable add-drop network. The proposed device consists of a resonator connected to two separate channels via optomechanical interfaces. By adjusting the connection states, the device can be customized to allow specific wavelengths to pass through, block others, or tap into the signal stream, making it an optimal choice for creating versatile optical networks. The proposed device's performance is demonstrated using numerical simulations.

The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted increased scrutiny of the effectiveness of public health initiatives. Social media and news outlets, filled with a diverse array of claims, present a challenge in separating fact from fiction. To combat misinformation, it is essential to understand the factors driving its dissemination and identify key initiatives that can mitigate its spread. To this end, researchers are exploring the use of social media and news to evaluate the success of public health initiatives and develop a model that can forecast the future spread of misinformation. Building on prior research, this study expands upon the news2indicators model by incorporating additional features from online news, such as the geographic distribution of news consumption and population demographics associated with specific news outlets. The model's performance is demonstrated through its analysis of the public health initiatives in Germany, highlighting the value of analyzing news consumption patterns and demographics in predicting the future spread of misinformation.

In various fields like image processing and data security, lossless image compression is a crucial technique. Although neural networks have made significant progress in this area, existing models are often not well-suited for GPU implementation, limiting their practical application. To address this issue, we propose PILC, a novel neural architecture for lossless image compression that is specifically optimized for real-time processing on GPUs. PILC combines a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) and a neural entropy calculator, utilizing a variational autoencoder approach with a latent vector. The CVAE employs a variational autoencoder model to encode images into low-dimensional vectors using a VAE, and a decoder to reconstruct the original image from these vectors. The CVAE outperforms previous methods in terms of lossless image compression, achieving a lower bit cost per pixel. The CVAE also features a decoder that can utilize a GPU to efficiently generate high-quality images. The PILC model is trained on the LJPBMC dataset and compared to other state-of-the-art compression methods, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Using proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at the interaction energies of 7 and 8 TeV with integrated luminosities of 1.0 and 2.0 inverse femtobarns, the $B^{+}$ meson is observed to decay into $D_s^{+}\phi$ with a significance of 5.4 standard deviations. A branching fraction measurement for the $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ decay is conducted, resulting in a specific branching fraction value of $(4.3\pm 0.5 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-4$. Additionally, the decay branching fraction of $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi$ is estimated as $(7.7 \pm 3.0 \pm 1.0 \pm 1.1 \pm 1.1 \pm \sqrt{\Gamma_{D_s\phi}/\Gamma_{D_s\phi (recoil)}$) times 10^{-4}, where the last error term accounts for the uncertainty related to the $D_s\phi$ meson width.

In a multi-agent learning scenario, we consider a group of agents that need to transfer knowledge from a set of experts to a learner. We assume that the learner is a neural network and the experts are labeled datasets. We also assume that the learner's knowledge distribution is influenced by a non-additive transfer function. Building upon previous research, we aim to find the most efficient way to train the learner by minimizing the expected loss while taking into account the uncertainty in the transfer function. We propose a new method called Optimal Transfer that achieves this goal by using a combination of outlier detection and regression techniques. We show that our method is robust against outliers and can be trained efficiently using a convex optimization problem. We also show that our method outperforms existing methods in a multi-agent learning scenario.

This paper suggests a novel method for training AI agents to collaborate effectively with humans in solving complex decision-making tasks. By incorporating the human choice model (HCM) into a Markov decision process (MDP), we can express the optimal collaboration strategy as a Markov process, allowing us to leverage reinforcement learning to train AI partners to make collaborative choices. Our approach yields AI partners that prioritize collaboration and maintain transparency, according to human subject evaluations. Furthermore, our method's ability to train agents with long-term, collaborative awareness also reveals potential for enhancing existing agents, thereby paving the way for the development of AI partners that work harmoniously with humans.

Researchers investigate a comprehensive supersymmetric model that incorporates a wide variety of particles, encompassing 27 distinct states, including 19 new ones. The model's structure allows these new states to be constrained by data from colliders, astrophysical observations, and cosmological theories. An in-depth analysis is conducted to determine the limits of heavy supersymmetric models, particularly in terms of the squarks, gluinos, gluon mediators, and other related particles. The study provides predictions for future searches at the LHC, an understanding of the dark matter composition, and the influence of the neutralino on the properties of the neutralino. The comprehensive model is thoroughly examined to reveal its intricately connected components.

This study investigates how individuals with diverse backgrounds and experience with visualizations complete tasks, particularly those requiring spatial reasoning. We recruited 384 participants from various fields and had them complete 14 tasks under controlled conditions. The results showed that, although profession had some impact, geology and neurology professionals performed similarly in tasks demanding spatial skills, whereas expertise and practice had more significant effects on task completion overall.

The issue of encoding inductive proofs has been a long-standing challenge for automated proof systems. Recent advancements have led to the creation of automated proof planners using dependency-based enrichment, which replicate inductive reasoning by reiteratively adding assumptions. Building on existing work, we've developed a method to enhance the induction step using a more comprehensive proof search strategy. Our approach incorporates a novel technique for analyzing and extracting valid logical arguments from the refinement graph, which involves identifying and incorporating clauses generated during the refinement process. By reusing these extracted clauses, we've effectively reduced the need for axiomatization, which is particularly beneficial in theories that are too complex for traditional axiomatization algorithms. We've evaluated our enhanced method in both geometric and field arithmetic proof systems and found it to significantly improve performance, resulting in a substantial increase in induction steps of up to 31% and overall completion times up to 52% less.

Graph retrieval is a critical issue in numerous applications, yet existing methods primarily focus on node and graph embeddings, neglecting the more refined task of aligning graphs for retrieval. This leads to less accurate graph matches and increased complexity in implementing rich retrieval models. We introduce the graph alignment problem in retrieval and present a novel model that generates embeddings reflecting actual graph similarities. Experimental evaluations on two real-world datasets indicate that our proposed model surpasses existing methods in effectiveness and complexity.

Deep learning models often struggle to accurately capture real-world applications when the input is far from the distribution seen during training. In this study, several techniques inspired by language modeling are applied to improve the performance of systems modeling continuous dynamics, such as stable neural control and forward dynamics models. We've found that pre-training, data augmentation, and over-parameterization can significantly enhance model accuracy in capturing real-world dynamics, especially in scenarios with limited available data.

A key challenge in distributing electricity in power systems lies in its current method of allocation, which uses complex graph algorithms with limited flexibility and inability to model external factors such as production and consumption. This study introduces a new distribution method based on mathematical principles, specifically the Jordan totient function, to meet these needs and is easily calculable. Additionally, the proposed method provides insights into network performance and is demonstrated through practical examples.

In the field of event-based research, particularly when examining complex and intricate events, it can be crucial to establish connections between individual event instances. We have developed a new approach to identify coreference events in large-scale collections, focusing on complex events that are often characterized by multiple viewpoints, conflicting perspectives, overlapping participants, and diverse levels of scope. This methodology is demonstrated through experiments conducted on two datasets, one related to protests and another focused on the 2016 US Presidential Election, with the findings indicating significant improvements in both cases.

We propose a straightforward yet comprehensive model for solving complementarity problems. By reformulating this issue as a standard linear program and subsequently a bin packing problem, our proposed approach can efficiently tackle large-scale problems, including those with thousands of variables and constraints. Furthermore, our model allows for the selection of a solution's essential aspects. We tested the approach using a large-scale instance of the linear programming relaxation of the geometric set covering problem, which involved 189 variables and 132 barriers, and achieved an accurate solution with only 0.1% of the variables in use.

Let $F$ be a field, $R$ a semiprime ring, and $0 \neq e \in U_{1}(R)$. We define an $(m, n)$-Jordan derivation, or centralizer, of $R$ with respect to $e$ by two specific formulas and examine their key properties. Moreover, we investigate how these tools interact with each other under various conditions.

We demonstrate that Weinberg's 2-factor theory arises as the most efficient solution to a theoretical framework based on spin constraints and a target space. This approach involves a specific quantum field theory on Minkowski space that incorporates a scalar field with a specific spin structure in its target space. The theory's two-dimensional action density is minimized such that it complies with the constraints without introducing additional degrees of freedom. The 2-factor theory is the optimal solution to this problem, and our work provides a theoretical explanation for the anomalies present in Weinberg's original theory.

We have developed an innovative framework for the transversal group of nonlinear projections. By doing so, we've identified and proven the equivalence of the transversal group to specific measures, including the nonlinear Hausdorff fractional dimension and a modified version of Favard's length. This work extends and provides an alternative to existing research, particularly that of H. Ostrovsky and S. Smale, and further refines the findings of H. Wu and R. Strichartz on nonlinear projections. Moreover, we've derived a pivotal inequality for the transversal group, which has numerous applications, including a nonlinear extension of the classic principle of inclusion-exclusion and a refined version of the existing fractional integration inequality.

To optimize controllers for complex, high-dimensional systems like quadrotors, a novel approach called Direct Policy Search has been developed, which offers significant improvements over model predictive control (MPC). However, existing methods in this area are hindered by high computational costs due to their reliance on complex functionals and gradient approximations. Our research presents a new method that minimizes the cost of a single function, a tube MPC error, by efficiently searching its space. Our approach is based on a detailed analysis of this function, which reveals that it is composed of smaller, linear components. Our method then uses these components to guide an optimization process, which benefits from lower-dimensional search spaces and linear optimization problems. Our research demonstrates that this approach is significantly more efficient than previous Direct Policy Search methods, with a notable 100 times improvement in the time it takes to find an optimal solution. Moreover, the optimization process is amenable to high-dimensional search spaces and can be completed within a millisecond, a significant improvement over the minutes required by existing methods.

Recent findings suggest that the intrinsic unusual Hall effect (IUE) can be explained by a quantum mechanism, specifically by the skew scattering effect, which occurs at the third order of the Born approximation in the Boltzmann equation. In this work, we investigate this IUE within the context of the generalized semiclassical theory (GSCT), a quantum Boltzmann transport theory, and discover that the GSCT naturally reproduces this IUE. Notably, we demonstrate that the IUE is reproduced at the third order of the GSCT, consistent with the Born approximation in the Boltzmann equation, and is unaffected by the phase relaxation time.
